---
title: "When Inquiry May Stop"
abstract: |
  Inquiry often ends with the discovery that the question one has been pursuing was defective, and that discovery is typically a result of pursuing it. This raises a problem that does not depend on any recent debate: when does an inquiry rightly end, and what does it take for it to have gone well? I defend a deliberately narrow thesis. Learning that a question is defective does not settle whether the inquirer may stop. Two inquirers in the same world, with the same question, the same defect and the same evidence, can differ in whether they may rationally stop, because they want different things from the answer. What decides is whether the trouble that made the question worth pursuing has been relieved by what the inquiry found. So no account of success or stopping stated over the asked question alone, including the recent norms against inquiring into defective questions, can be complete. I defend this against two objections, that the inquirer's "real question" was always bigger and that success is just the clearing of her agenda, and I say what is left of the thesis if each is granted.
bibliography: dissolving-questions.bib
format:

# The problem {#sec-problem}

Inquiries end in many ways. One, familiar from every discipline, is that the inquirer finds out that the question she has been pursuing was the wrong one. It takes for granted something false, or an answer to it would not give her what she wanted. This ending has two features that make it philosophically awkward. First, the discovery that a question is defective is typically a result of inquiring into it: one finds out that there is no such thing by looking for it. Second, the discovery leaves open what to do next. Sometimes it is the end of the matter. Sometimes it is the start of the real work.

So here is the problem. When may an inquirer who has found a defect in her question rightly stop, and what does it take for an inquiry that ended that way to have gone well?

The problem would exist if no one had written about it recently. Dewey observes that "Inquiry and questioning, up to a certain point, are synonymous terms" [@dewey1938, 105], and the qualification is the problem. Peirce takes inquiry to begin with the irritation of doubt, so that "with the cessation of doubt it ends," and he insists that merely putting a proposition in interrogative form starts nothing: "There must be a real and living doubt" [@peirce1877, sec. IV]. Collingwood notes that a question can fail to "arise" because the presupposition it involves is not being made [@collingwood1940, 26]. Laudan notes that problems can "simply vanish from a given domain" when beliefs about what is happening change [@laudan1977, 35--36]. None of them asks what a good ending to an inquiry into a defective question consists in.

Recent epistemology gives the problem a sharp form. It models inquiry as an interrogative attitude toward a question, and it states norms of inquiry over questions. I shall call this the question-first picture. The recent papers that build it out, and the papers that complicate it, are the occasion of what follows and not its subject. I use them as the best statement of a view on which the question determines how the inquiry is to be assessed, and I say in @sec-prior how much of what I say they have already said.

My thesis has three parts, in increasing order of controversy.

1. *Underdetermination.* Whether an inquirer who has learned that her question is defective may rationally stop is not fixed by the question, its defect, the evidence, or the facts of the case. Different purposes with the same question can give different verdicts (@sec-pair).
2. *What decides.* It is decided by whether the trouble that made the question worth pursuing has been relieved by what the inquiry found. A question is a proposal about how to relieve a trouble, and the inquiry is individuated by the trouble (@sec-problems).
3. *Consequence.* An account of success or stopping that is stated over the asked question alone cannot be complete. The norms against inquiring into defective questions are not accounts of when inquiry may end, and they cannot be converted into one (@sec-norms).

I do not claim that the norms are false, or that the inquiry into a defective question is always permissible. I claim they are silent on the matter this paper is about.

# The question-first picture {#sec-picture}

The orthodox starting point is that inquiry is directed at answering a question. On J. Friedman's account, "in inquiring into some question we aim to resolve or answer the question," and when it goes well "we settle some matter that previously was or felt unsettled to us" [@friedman2017, 307; @friedman2019, sec. 1]. Peacocke begins from the definition: "To inquire into some question Q is to try to answer Q" [@peacocke2026, abstract]. The norms built on this are stated over questions.

- *Don't Believe and Inquire:* one ought not inquire into Q at a time and also believe a complete answer to Q at that time [@friedman2019].
- *No Defective Questions* and the *Knowledge Norm for Inquiry:* one ought to inquire into an unconditional question only if it has a true, complete and direct answer, and in the stronger version only if one knows that it has one [@willardkyle2023]. A question is defective when one of its presuppositions is false.
- *Sound Question Norm:* it is irrational to wonder Q while one's knowledge does not entail all of Q's presuppositions. Its authors present it as "proof of concept" for a research program in erotetic logic, say that they do not aim to adjudicate its plausibility, and say that it offers evaluations and not blame [@whitcombmillson2024].
- *Norms against pseudo-questions:* "In inquiring into Q, one aims at finding the true answer to Q," and there is none to find if Q relies on false presuppositions [@rosa2025]. Palmira endorses a factive evaluative norm, that there is something good about inquiry that can deliver knowledgeable answers to the questions under investigation and something bad about inquiry that cannot [@palmira2026].

Several authors resist these norms for uncertain inquirers. Falbo defends a weak necessary condition: inquiry is permissible only if it is not rational to be sure that it will not improve one's epistemic position on the question [@falbo2024]. Hubacher Haerle derives a Success Norm from the thought that inquiries are actions, and notes that "I might need to first inquire for a while before I realize that the question I'm after has no answer" [@hubacherhaerle2026]. Khalifa and Millson hold that true corrective answers to questions with false presuppositions are epistemically valuable, and that such questions "can be engines of good inquiry" [@khalifamillson2020]. D. Friedman's Intention Account, on which an inquirer intends to answer a question by forming a settled attitude toward a complete answer, does not discuss defective questions [@friedmand2025].

Three things are common ground. Norms govern attitudes and actions that are individuated by their question. An inquiry that reaches its question's answer has succeeded. And the status of an inquiry into a defective question is a matter of how it stands to that question. The first is harmless. The second is true in the central case. The third is what I shall deny.

# The same world, different purposes {#sec-pair}

**The shortfall.** Ines manages a café. The Friday till is £200 short. She asks: which of my three cashiers took it? She watches the till, reconciles receipts and talks to staff. The case is constructed to isolate one feature. In version A she finds that a cash payment to a supplier was entered twice on Thursday's sheet; the till was never short. In version B the till is short and the receipts reconcile, and the security camera shows the supplier's driver lifting the cash from the open drawer while the cashier was in the stock room. Nothing suggests that anyone helped him.

In both versions the question has a false presupposition, and Ines learns that no cashier took the money. In A she may stop. Her trouble is gone, she knows why, and nothing is left to settle. In B she may not. She has learned something, but money is gone and she does not know how or whom to pursue. To treat the matter as closed would be to give up, not to finish. Only when she asks about the driver, and settles that, has she done what she set out to do. The corrective answer is the same in both, so the answer cannot be what separates them.

A question-first theorist can reply that the worlds differ, and that in B there is a further question about the driver which Ines has not answered. That reply is available, and I come back to it in @sec-bigger. To see what it costs, hold the world fixed.

**The auditor.** Keep version B. The café's owner has a standing policy that any shortfall traced to a member of staff triggers a disciplinary review. She sends an auditor, Tomás, whose only task is to decide whether the policy applies. He too asks which cashier took the money, and uses the same checks. He learns what Ines learns, that no cashier did. He reports that the policy does not apply, and he may stop. His job is finished. Ines, in the same world with the same evidence, still has her work to do.

Ines and Tomás ask the same question. They have the same defect, the same corrective answer, the same evidence and the same world. They differ only in what they wanted to be rid of: Ines wants to know what became of the money, and Tomás wants to know whether to open a review. One may stop and the other may not. So the defect of the question, together with everything about the question and the facts, does not tell you when it is rational to stop. That is the underdetermination thesis.

# A real pair of stages: Mercury {#sec-mercury}

The shortfall is constructed. Here is a case I can document from two primary texts. I use only what those texts say and make no claim about the history between them.

In 1859 Le Verrier wrote to Faye about the motion of Mercury's perihelion. He had found that the observations required an additional 38 seconds of arc per century. He first asked what change in the masses of the known planets would produce it, and found that it could be done only by increasing the mass attributed to Venus by at least a tenth. Then he checked this against the Earth's obliquity, from which the mass of Venus can also be inferred, and found that the two appeared to imply different masses: "Un embarras sérieux résulte donc de la comparaison des théories de la Terre et de Mercure." If the obliquity result were accepted, he wrote, one would be led to think the excess due to "quelque action encore inconnue," and he considered a planet between Mercury and the Sun, and then a ring of small bodies. He added: "Je n'ai nullement l'intention de décider d'une manière absolue entre ces hypothèses. J'ai voulu seulement établir qu'il y a là une grave difficulté" [@leverrier1859, 381--383].

So the question "by how much must Venus's mass be changed?" was retired by what pursuing it found. The inquiry was not over. Le Verrier replaced the question with another, about unseen matter, considered as a better means to the same end, which was to account for the excess. The trouble persisted through the change of question. This is the B side of the pair.

In November 1915 Einstein reported that his new theory of gravitation accounts for "die von Leverrier entdeckte säkulare Drehung der Merkurbahn," about 45 seconds of arc per century, "qualitativ und quantitativ," and does so "ohne daß irgendwelche besondere Hypothese zugrunde gelegt werden müßte": without any special hypothesis having to be assumed. The calculation gives 43 seconds per century, where the astronomers give 45 ± 5 as the "unerklärten Rest zwischen Beobachtungen und NEWTONScher Theorie." Einstein's verdict is "volle Übereinstimmung," full agreement [@einstein1915, 831, 839]. This is the A side. The question of what unseen matter perturbs Mercury was not answered. It was not refuted either, in any way that mattered to the people who took the theory on. It lost its point, because the trouble it served was relieved by something else. A norm against inquiring into a question with a false presupposition has nothing to say about why that is a good ending. A success condition stated as answering the question calls it a failure.

Two cautions. First, the defect of the unseen-matter question, if it is one, was not found by pursuing that question. It was found, if at all, through the success of a theory built for other reasons. So the case does not support the claim that defects are found by pursuing the question they infect. Second, Einstein's text shows that a community could treat the 1859 trouble as relieved. It does not show what any individual's inquiry aimed at. For individuals I rely on the constructed pair.

# What the norms can and cannot say {#sec-norms}

**Attitudes and activities.** The norms govern interrogative attitudes. Ines wonders which cashier took the money while her knowledge does not entail the presupposition. If the Sound Question Norm is true she is irrational at that moment, in A and in B. This is a verdict on what she wonders at a time. It does not say when she may stop. Stopping is a transition between states, and a norm on wondering a question does not say whether the transition is permissible. J. Friedman makes the same point about a different case: knowing the answer does not itself end an inquiry, because "Ending my inquiry would be a separate step, not one identical to or necessitated by my getting the relevant piece of knowledge" [@friedman2024aim, sec. 2.2]. The same goes for learning that the question is defective.

**Continuing.** One norm does govern continuing. Once one realizes that a question has a false presupposition, "further inquiry into Q would be irrational or otherwise epistemically inappropriate" [@friedman2017, 315--316]. I accept this, and it is not idle after the discovery. It tells Ines, in both versions, to stop asking which cashier took the money. But it says the same to Tomás, to Ines in A and to Ines in B. It cannot mark the difference between them. Willard-Kyle's advice, that having discovered the defect "we stop asking it, revising our question if necessary" [@willardkyle2023, sec. 6], puts the weight on "if necessary." When is revising necessary? Nothing in the question or its defect says.

**Objective standards.** Palmira and Rosa respond to the worry that the norms demand what an uncertain inquirer cannot know. Palmira's norm is evaluative, a standard of goodness and not of permission. Rosa's norms concern the goal constitutive of inquiring, and he says the "should" is not all-things-considered. I grant the point. An evaluative standard of the form "this is a bad question to be wondering" can be true without guiding anyone. But it is silent about stopping, and it owes an account of what it evaluates. Palmira's version says there is something good about inquiry that can deliver knowledgeable answers to the questions under investigation. Tomás's inquiry could not deliver a knowledgeable direct answer to his question, and it is not a bad inquiry. It did what it was for. If the evaluative norm is read as being about direct answers, it rates model discoveries as deficient. If it is read as being about whatever the inquirer needed, the factive "answer to Q" has dropped out.

**Discovery.** Hubacher Haerle already presses the point that norms requiring knowledge that Q is sound block the inquiry through which unsoundness is found, and Falbo presses the point that such norms are overly restrictive for inquirers who start from mistaken or confused premises. I accept both points and do not add to them. I add something narrower. Weakening the norms to permissions, as they do, leaves untouched the question I am asking, because a permission to begin does not say when to end. Hubacher Haerle's reply to the alchemists who sought an elixir and found gunpowder is that "as soon as scientists notice that there is no epistemic improvement to be had on Q, they should switch to Q*." This is the nearest thing to a stopping norm in the work I discuss. It says to switch. It does not say to what, or when switching is not needed. Tomás need not switch.

**Degrees.** The norms speak of knowing that a presupposition is false. Real inquiries move through degrees. Le Verrier did not claim to know that the Venus-mass route was closed, and declined to "décider d'une manière absolue" among the hypotheses. A norm that triggers at knowledge does not govern the long middle, and it is in the middle that the question whether to go on is live. What the inquirer needs there is not a verdict about the question but a view of how much of her trouble remains.

**Redescription.** One might say Ines should have asked a different question, whether any cashier took it. This is what Falbo calls a question with easy entailments, and she objects that the strategy is "ad hoc and psychologically unrealistic" [@falbo2024]. D. Friedman reports the same worry about redescription in the case of double-checking, and does not rely on it [@friedmand2025]. Add a dilemma. Ines's activity is the same whichever question we say she pursues. Her checks do not come in two versions. If the redescription is a relabeling of one activity, the norm constrains the labels and not the inquiry. If it is not, the norm forbids the activity. Either way it does not say when she may stop.

# Two replies I take seriously {#sec-replies}

## The question was always bigger {#sec-bigger}

The strongest reply says that Ines's real question was never "which cashier?" but "what happened to the money?", or "what, if anything, accounts for the apparent shortfall?" That is a sound question, her inquiry succeeds if and only if it is answered, and the norms apply to it. In A she answers it. In B she is still working on it. Tomás's real question is "does the policy apply?"

One might answer that the bigger question has no answer space until the inquiry has produced the concepts to state it. That answer fails. On the standard conceptions a question is individuated by its answers, as a set of propositions or a partition of the space of possibilities [@whitcombmillson2024], and such an object exists whether or not the inquirer can list its members. She can wonder "what accounts for the shortfall?" without listing the candidates. So that answer is not available.

There is a second difficulty, for me. By my own definition "What happened to the money?" is itself defective in version A, where nothing happened to the money: the till was never short. The repair is to a question that builds in a place for the unexpected, something like "what, if anything, accounts for the shortfall, and is there one?" But a question with a built-in "none of these" answer is sound whatever the facts. Soundness is then free, and norms that require it are met by weakening the question. Worse, the catch-all answer is the same in A and B. In B "something other than a cashier" is a complete answer to the enlarged question and Ines has not finished. Corrective answers are the answers Khalifa and Millson say carry epistemic value, and I agree that they do. But a corrective answer is the same in A and B, so to count it as the resolution of an enlarged question is to call B a success.

So I accept that a bigger question is always available. I accept the regress, and I say what is left. First, the question that fixes success is not the asked question, and it is not any function of the asked question and its defect, such as the enlargement by a catch-all cell. A and B receive the same answer to every such enlargement. It is fixed by the trouble, and its cells are the ways the trouble might or might not be relieved. This is what I call the problem, in question form. If someone wishes to say that the problem is the bigger question, I have no objection. Second, the norms as stated in the literature are stated over the question the inquirer is asking. Ines can wonder "which cashier?" in service of the bigger question, and that is not irrational. So either the Sound Question Norm is violated by an ordinary good inquirer, or it is not about the question that fixes the success of her inquiry. Third, the content of the success-fixing question varies with the inquirer's purpose, as Ines and Tomás show. A semantics that gives the same content to both attitudes cannot say when each may stop. One that makes content sensitive to purpose has conceded the point.

What remains of the thesis, then, is this. The unit that fixes success and stopping is a purpose-fixed question that the asked question serves. It is not recoverable from the asked question and its defect, and the norms stated over the asked question are not norms for it. That is narrower than a thesis about success in general, and I think it is true.

## Success is just clearing the agenda {#sec-agenda}

The second reply is more dangerous because it is nearly my view. On this view an inquiry has gone well when the inquirer's open agenda has been cleared. In A nothing is left open. In B "who, or how?" remains. For Tomás nothing remains. This is neutral about problems and uses only the idea that interrogative attitudes put questions on an agenda, which is common ground.

I agree with the verdicts, and I accept that if the agenda is read as what the inquirer is rationally to be wondering, my view and this one agree. What I deny is that the agenda view is complete. It needs two things it does not supply.

*Which items belong after the discovery.* The agenda of Ines in B, after she has learned that no cashier took the money, contains "who took it, and how?" That item is not a consequence of what she learned, or of the question she asked. It is on her agenda because of what she wants. Tomás learns the same thing and the item is not on his. If the agenda is just the set of questions the inquirer is in fact wondering, then Ines in B who, tired, fails to notice that anything is left has a clear agenda and has not succeeded. If it is the set of questions she should be wondering, what fixes it is her purpose.

*When an item is discharged without being answered.* Agenda items leave by being answered, by being deleted, or by being discharged. Tomás's "which cashier?" is discharged by learning that there is none, because what it was for is done. The question of what unseen matter perturbs Mercury is discharged by a theory that makes the matter unnecessary. Neither is deleted, since deletion is abandonment and would count against the inquirer, and neither is answered. The only uniform rule for discharge I can find is: an item is discharged when what it was for no longer needs doing. That rule mentions the purpose.

So I do not take the agenda view as a rival. Suitably qualified, it is my view in other words, and I have no reason to resist the label "clearing the right agenda." What the problem view adds is the source of the items and the rule for discharge, and two further conditions that the agenda view lacks, that the clearing be due to what the inquiry found and that it leave the inquirer epistemically well placed. Without them the agenda view cannot tell success from the cheap ways of clearing an agenda, which are deleting, forgetting and never noticing.

# Problems {#sec-problems}

People ask questions in order to do something about something: to remove a puzzle, restore an equilibrium, make a decision, explain an anomaly. Call the thing to be done about something a *problem*. It consists of a *trouble*, a state of the inquirer that she wants to be rid of (an unexplained datum, a conflict among her commitments, a decision that cannot be made on what she knows), and a *standard of relief*, which says what would count as being rid of it. A question is a proposal about how to meet the standard: if I knew the answer to Q, the trouble would go. At any stage the inquirer has a current question, pursued as the best available means. When it proves defective, or no longer the best means, she changes it.

This is close to Peirce's doubt and Dewey's problematic situation. Dewey's "A problem represents the partial transformation by inquiry of a problematic situation into a determinate situation" is nearly the definition [@dewey1938, 108], and Peirce's irritation of doubt is a trouble of the epistemic kind [@peirce1877]. It differs from Laudan's, whose empirical problems are presumed states of affairs and are "solved" when scientists "properly no longer regard it as an unanswered question" [@laudan1977, 22]. My trouble is a state of the inquirer, and the Mercury excess is a trouble for astronomers because they wish to account for it. The relation to Laudan is close: a solved problem is not an answered question.

**Individuation.** Stages under different questions Q and Q′ belong to one inquiry when Q′ was adopted in light of what was found while pursuing Q, and as a better means to relieve the trouble Q was adopted to relieve. A test for the second condition: if she learned the answer to Q′ would she count the trouble as relieved, and if she had learned an answer to Q alone would she have counted it as unrelieved? For Ines in B, yes to both, and for Le Verrier too.

**Success.** An inquiry succeeds when it ends in a state in which (i) the trouble is relieved by the standard of relief the inquirer began with, or by a revision of it that she can defend on the basis of what the inquiry found; (ii) the relief is due to what the inquiry found and not to luck, forgetting or the passage of time; and (iii) her state is epistemically good: she knows or understands what the relief rests on. She is then rationally able to stop. Relief comes in degrees, and so does the rationality of stopping. Where some trouble remains she may rationally stop when what is left is not worth the cost of pursuit, and then she has stopped short of full success but not abandoned the inquiry. Where she can see that the trouble remains and stops anyway for no such reason, she has abandoned it.

*Answering as a special case.* When the trouble is the open question itself, relief is knowing the answer, and the view agrees with the question-first picture where that is plausible. It differs where the question is a proposal about how to meet a trouble and proves a bad one.

*Moving the goalposts.* The danger is that any inquirer who fails to answer her question can claim success by redescribing what she wanted. Three constraints guard against it. The trouble and its standard of relief are fixed by her reasons for beginning, which are independent of how things turn out. The relief must come from what the inquiry found. And the end state must be epistemically good: someone who mistakenly believes the presupposition false and stops has not succeeded, whatever she feels. A revision of the standard is permitted only when what the inquiry found gives her a reason to make it.

# Is the dispute verbal? {#sec-verbal}

A defender of the question-first picture can accept every verdict above and decline to give up the word. Ines in A, on this view, has a "failed inquiry" in Willard-Kyle's phrase, from which she learned and was right to stop [@willardkyle2023, sec. 6]. Success is answering, and the rest is vocabulary.

I want to say exactly what is at stake, because there are three distinct things.

*What the opponent must accept.* A question-first theorist who agrees that Tomás may stop and Ines may not must say that the status of the inquiry depends on something other than the question, the defect and the world. That is the underdetermination thesis. She may call the something else "what the inquirer wanted," or "the bigger question," or "the agenda." On each the unit that settles when to stop is individuated by purpose and not by the content of the asked question. The alternative is to say that Tomás must continue, which no one believes. This is a substantive consequence, not a relabeling, because it determines what a theory of the attitude and its norms has to be able to represent.

*Why a success notion should track stopping.* The residual dispute is whether "success" should be the status that tracks when an inquiry may stop. I think it should, for two reasons. First, an inquiry does not end of itself on reaching what it sought. J. Friedman argues that the verbs for inquiring are atelic, so that reaching the inquirer's terminus does not make continuing impossible [@friedman2024aim, sec. 2.2]. A theory of inquiry therefore owes an account of when to end, and the natural place for it is the account of success. Peacocke begins from the thought that to understand inquiry "we must understand what constitutes success in this endeavor" [@peacocke2026, abstract]. I share the thought and add that the success so understood must be the status that tells us when to end. Second, a notion on which Ines in A and Tomás fail, and on which Ines in B before she asks about the driver fails in the same sense, marks no difference that anyone needs.

*The aim of inquiry.* So the dispute reduces, in the end, to a claim about what inquiry aims at: finding the true answer to the question asked, or relieving the trouble the question served by what is found. I do not need a full theory of aims. J. Friedman is skeptical of "the aim of inquiry" as a structural claim and argues that inquirers' personal aims vary, as the aims of Watson and Crick might have varied, without their ceasing to be inquirers [@friedman2024aim, sec. 3]. If the aim is personal, it is the trouble, and Ines and Tomás have different aims in asking the same question. If it is structural, as in Rosa's "In inquiring into Q, one aims at finding the true answer to Q," then Tomás's inquiry is "bound to fail to achieve its own aim" [@rosa2025], and he rightly stops. The aim claim then does no work in telling us when to stop. Either way the work is done by the problem.

**What would show me wrong.**

1. A way to determine from the question alone, without appeal to the inquirer's purposes, which of Ines and Tomás may stop. Enlarging the answer space does not do it, since both get the same corrective answer. I do not think anything will, but a theory that did would defeat the thesis.
2. A convincing case of rational retirement where, afterward, nothing in the inquirer's situation can be described as a trouble relieved or persisting.
3. A principled account of problems on which my constraints against moving the goalposts fail, so that any inquiry can be reclassified as a success.

# Closest prior work, and what this adds {#sec-prior}

*Permissibility and success.* The nearest work is on whether inquiry into a question that lacks a true answer can be permissible or valuable. Falbo's Epistemic Improvement norm lets the value of inquiry exceed answering [@falbo2024]. Palmira resolves a puzzle about defective inquiry by separating evaluative from prescriptive norms [@palmira2026]. Rosa defends a norm against inquiry into pseudo-questions and answers the objection that such inquiry can pay off [@rosa2025]. Hubacher Haerle's Success Norm makes success explicit, and his model of epistemic improvement is, by his own account, narrow: improving a conceptual framework "cannot be captured by the ruling out of possible worlds," and he leaves a wider notion to future work [@hubacherhaerle2026]. Khalifa and Millson come closest to my target. They hold that false presuppositions need not make a question irrelevant, since such questions can be "engines of good inquiry" by producing corrective answers or by implying other questions [@khalifamillson2020]. Their concern is epistemic value, not stopping, and they keep the answer to the question as the locus of value. The thesis that inquiry into a defective question can be permissible and valuable is theirs and not mine.

*Ancestors.* Peirce's irritation of doubt is the nearest ancestor of the trouble: inquiry begins and ends with it. Peirce notes that "as soon as a firm belief is reached we are entirely satisfied, whether the belief be true or false," and goes on to rank methods of fixing belief by whether doubt can return. The relief of a trouble does not by itself distinguish success from comfortable self-deception, and my conditions (ii) and (iii) play, for a single inquiry, a role like that ranking [@peirce1877]. Dewey's problematic situation is the more developed ancestor, and I have not tried to reproduce his account of its determination [@dewey1938]. Collingwood's point that a question can fail to arise relative to what is supposed is the ancestor of defect-relativity; he says that the "logical efficacy of a supposition does not depend upon the truth of what is supposed" but on its being supposed [@collingwood1940, ch. 4, prop. 3], and he does not discuss the end of inquiry. Laudan supplies the parallel between solved problems and answered questions [@laudan1977].

*Questions and answers.* The terminology of presuppositions and corrective answers is Belnap's, in van Fraassen's statement: a correction is "any denial of any presupposition" of the question [@vanfraassen1980, 140].

*What is new.* Narrowly: the same-world pair showing that the stopping verdict is underdetermined by question, defect and evidence; the diagnosis that the two best replies, the bigger question and the cleared agenda, each concede that the unit of success is purpose-fixed; the discharge rule for agenda items; and the Mercury pair as a documented case. I do not claim that retiring questions is new, that inquiry into defective questions can be reasonable, or that inquiry is organized by trouble and not by question. Peacocke and D. Friedman state the view I oppose in its most careful form, that inquiry is trying to answer a question or intending to [@peacocke2026; @friedmand2025], and I take no stand on the problems they raise about what answering is.

# Conclusion

When an inquirer learns that the question she has been pursuing is defective, one of two things is true. She has relieved what prompted it, and may rest, or she has not, and must go on, with another question. Which holds is not decided by the question or by the defect. It is decided by the problem. The norms that forbid inquiry into defective questions may be right about what to wonder. They do not say when to stop, and they cannot be turned into a statement of it, because the same question, defect and evidence can end one inquiry and merely redirect another.
